summaryBox.takeaway: Prokaryotes reproduce vegetatively by binary fission. Genetic variation is introduced via Horizontal Gene Transfer (Transformation, Conjugation, and Transduction) without true gametic syngamy.

conceptBreakdown.content: Prokaryotes reproduce primarily via asexual division. True eukaryotic sexual reproduction (involving syngamy and meiosis) is absent. Instead, genetic variation is introduced through Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT) / Para-sexual Recombination.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 3.1 Asexual Reproduction & Endospore Formation
conceptBreakdown.title: 3.1 Asexual Reproduction & Endospore Formation
conceptBreakdown.content:
• Binary Fission: Primary vegetative propagation mechanism under favorable nutrient conditions. The circular chromosome undergoes semi-conservative replication anchored to cell membrane mesosomes, followed by centripetal wall septation.

• Endospores: Formed inside Gram-positive vegetative cells (*Bacillus*, *Clostridium*) under extreme nutrient starvation.
- Resistance Factors: Endospores survive boiling (100°C for hours), gamma radiation, chemical disinfectants, and desiccation.
- Biochemical Basis: The core contains Calcium Dipicolinate (Calcium-Dipicolinic Acid complex [Ca-DPA]), which dehydrates the spore cytoplasm (10–30% water content) and stabilizes DNA against thermal denaturation. High concentration of Small Acid-Soluble Spore Proteins (SASPs) bound to DNA.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 3.2 Mechanisms of Parasexual Recombination
conceptBreakdown.title: 3.2 Mechanisms of Parasexual Recombination
conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
CONJUGATION MECHANISMS
                           
    1. F⁺ × F⁻ CROSS
       F⁺ Donor (Plasmid Free in Cytoplasm) + F⁻ Recipient ──► TWO F⁺ CELLS
       
    2. Hfr × F⁻ CROSS
       Hfr Donor (F-Plasmid Integrated into Chromosome) + F⁻ Recipient
       ──► Transfer of chromosomal genes; Recipient remains F⁻ (usually)
conceptBreakdown.content:
A. Transformation:
• Discovered by Frederick Griffith (1928) in *Streptococcus pneumoniae*; molecular basis proved by Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty (1944).
• Process by which a physiologically competent bacterial cell takes up naked, extracellular DNA fragments from its surrounding liquid medium and integrates them into its chromosome via homologous recombination.

B. Conjugation:
• Discovered by Lederberg and Tatum (1946) in *Escherichia coli*.
• Direct transfer of genetic material between two living bacterial cells through a physical conjugation bridge (Sex Pilus), encoded by the F-plasmid (Fertility Factor).
• 1. F⁺ × F⁻ Cross: F⁺ donor transfers plasmid copy to F⁻ recipient; both become F⁺.
• 2. Hfr × F⁻ Cross: High Frequency of Recombination donor transfers high-yield chromosomal genes; recipient typically remains F⁻.

C. Transduction:
• Discovered by Zinder and Lederberg (1952) in *Salmonella typhimurium*.
• Transfer of bacterial host DNA from one cell to another mediated by a bacteriophage (viral) vector.
1. Generalized Transduction: Occurs during the lytic cycle; random bacterial DNA fragments are accidentally packaged inside the phage capsid.
2. Specialized Transduction: Occurs during the lysogenic cycle; temperate phage (e.g., Lambda phage) excises imprecisely from the host chromosome, carrying specific adjacent host genes (e.g., *gal* or *bio* operons) to the recipient cell.
